cards.front: What does glycolysis make from one glucose?
cards.back: Two three-carbon pyruvate molecules, a little ATP, and NADH (banked electrons). It also hands carbon building blocks to the rest of the cell.
cards.quote: It splits one glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules, earns a little ATP, banks electrons as NADH

cards.front: When can a kinase load a phosphate onto ADP favorably?
cards.back: Only when the donor phosphate is more eager to leave than ATP's own, that is, higher than ATP on the phosphoryl-transfer ladder.
cards.why: So glycolysis must build phosphates above ATP before it can earn any ATP.
cards.quote: A kinase, an enzyme that moves a phosphate group, can load ADP favorably only from a phosphate more eager to leave than ATP's own

cards.front: A phosphate has a more negative standard free energy of hydrolysis (ΔG°′). Where does it sit on the phosphoryl-transfer ladder?
cards.back: Higher: the more negative ΔG°′, the higher its phosphoryl-transfer potential.
cards.quote: The more negative the value, the higher the phosphate sits on the ladder (its phosphoryl-transfer potential).
cards.section: A ladder of phosphates

cards.front: Rank from highest to lowest phosphoryl-transfer potential: ATP, glucose-6-phosphate, phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), phosphocreatine, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
cards.back: PEP > 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate > phosphocreatine > ATP > glucose-6-phosphate.
cards.quote: Glycolysis must build phosphates above ATP.
cards.section: A ladder of phosphates

cards.front: ΔG°′ of hydrolysis is −61.9 kJ/mol for PEP and −30.5 kJ/mol for ATP. What is ΔG°′ for PEP + ADP → pyruvate + ATP?
cards.back: Donor minus acceptor: −61.9 − (−30.5) = −31.4 kJ/mol, strongly favorable.
cards.quote: PEP to ADP (step 10): −61.9 − (−30.5) = −31.4 kJ/mol, strongly favorable.
cards.section: A ladder of phosphates

cards.front: ΔG°′ of hydrolysis is −13.8 kJ/mol for glucose-6-phosphate and −30.5 kJ/mol for ATP. Could glucose-6-phosphate phosphorylate ADP? Give ΔG°′.
cards.back: No. −13.8 − (−30.5) = +16.7 kJ/mol, unfavorable: an ordinary phosphate ester cannot make ATP. (The reverse, ATP to glucose, is −16.7.)
cards.quote: Run backward, glucose-6-phosphate to ADP, it is +16.7: an ordinary phosphate ester cannot make ATP.
cards.section: A ladder of phosphates

cards.front: What does hexokinase do at step 1 of glycolysis?
cards.back: It moves a phosphate from ATP onto carbon 6 of glucose, making glucose-6-phosphate. The negative charge traps it in the cell.
cards.quote: Hexokinase moves a phosphate from ATP onto carbon 6 of glucose.
cards.section: Investment, steps 1–5: trap, reshape, commit, split

cards.front: What would go wrong if hexokinase did not close around glucose by induced fit?
cards.back: Water could reach the active site, so ATP's phosphate could go to water (wasted hydrolysis) instead of to glucose.
cards.quote: It closes around glucose by induced fit, which keeps water out, so ATP's phosphate goes to glucose and not to water.
cards.section: Investment, steps 1–5: trap, reshape, commit, split

cards.front: A patient receives an ¹⁸F-labeled glucose analog and a PET scan shows bright spots in some tumors. Why does the label accumulate there?
cards.back: The analog is phosphorylated at step 1 and trapped in the cell, so tissues that take up glucose fast, including many tumors, collect the most label.
cards.quote: an ¹⁸F-labeled glucose analog is trapped after step 1, so tissues that take up glucose fast, including many tumors, light up.
cards.section: Investment, steps 1–5: trap, reshape, commit, split

cards.front: Aldolase cuts the bond between the carbon next to the carbonyl and the one after it. If phosphoglucose isomerase were skipped and the carbonyl stayed on carbon 1, what pieces would the cut give?
cards.back: A two-carbon and a four-carbon piece (cut between carbons 2 and 3), not two three-carbon halves. Moving the carbonyl to carbon 2 puts the cut between carbons 3 and 4 and frees carbon 1 for the second phosphate.
cards.quote: With it at carbon 1, the cut would fall between carbons 2 and 3: a two-carbon and a four-carbon piece.
cards.section: Investment, steps 1–5: trap, reshape, commit, split

cards.front: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis, and why is it called committed?
cards.back: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1, step 3), which makes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Its product is dedicated to glycolysis.
cards.quote: This is the committed step: its product is dedicated to glycolysis.
cards.section: Investment, steps 1–5: trap, reshape, commit, split

cards.front: What two products does aldolase make from fructose-1,6-bisphosphate?
cards.back: Two three-carbon pieces, each with one phosphate: dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP).
cards.quote: Aldolase cuts it into two three-carbon pieces, each with one phosphate: dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP).
cards.section: Investment, steps 1–5: trap, reshape, commit, split

cards.front: Triose phosphate isomerase is completely blocked, so DHAP cannot become GAP. Per glucose, what are the net ATP and NADH yields?
cards.back: Net 0 ATP and 1 NADH. Only one GAP per glucose runs the payoff: steps 7 and 10 make 2 ATP, which only repay the 2 spent at steps 1 and 3; step 6 runs once.
cards.why: Rests on TPI making the halves identical and on the doubling from step 6 onward.
cards.quote: Only GAP has the aldehyde that step 6 oxidizes, so without TPI half the carbon would be stranded.
cards.section: Investment, steps 1–5: trap, reshape, commit, split

cards.front: Why does every glycolytic yield from step 6 onward count double per glucose?
cards.back: Aldolase splits the six-carbon sugar into two halves and TPI makes both of them GAP, so each later step runs twice per glucose.
cards.quote: Both halves now run the same steps, so every yield from step 6 onward counts double
cards.section: Investment, steps 1–5: trap, reshape, commit, split

cards.front: What happens at step 6 of glycolysis (GAPDH)?
cards.back: GAPDH oxidizes GAP's aldehyde carbon (carbon 1); NAD⁺ takes the electrons and becomes NADH. The product is 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
cards.quote: GAPDH oxidizes GAP's aldehyde carbon (carbon 1), and NAD⁺ takes the electrons to become NADH.
cards.section: Payoff, steps 6–10: make a phosphate worth more than ATP's, then cash it

cards.front: How does GAPDH save the energy of the aldehyde oxidation instead of losing it as heat?
cards.back: An active-site cysteine bonds the aldehyde, so oxidation leaves an activated thioester on the enzyme. Inorganic phosphate (not ATP) then attacks it, giving the acyl phosphate 1,3-BPG.
cards.quote: an active-site cysteine first bonds to the aldehyde, so the oxidation leaves a thioester, an activated bond, on the enzyme.
cards.section: Payoff, steps 6–10: make a phosphate worth more than ATP's, then cash it

cards.front: ΔG°′ of hydrolysis is −49.3 kJ/mol for 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and −30.5 kJ/mol for ATP. From these, what is ΔG°′ for the phosphoglycerate kinase reaction (step 7)?
cards.back: −49.3 − (−30.5) = −18.8 kJ/mol. The tabulated value is −18.5; standard values differ slightly by source.
cards.quote: which is also why the ladder arithmetic gives −18.8 for step 7 against the table's −18.5
cards.section: About the free-energy table

cards.front: What is substrate-level phosphorylation?
cards.back: One enzyme passes a phosphate from a substrate directly to ADP, with no mitochondrion, oxygen or membrane gradient. Steps 7 and 10 of glycolysis work this way.
cards.quote: This is substrate-level phosphorylation: one enzyme passes a phosphate from a substrate to ADP, with no mitochondrion, oxygen or membrane gradient.
cards.section: Payoff, steps 6–10: make a phosphate worth more than ATP's, then cash it

cards.front: Why do steps 8 and 9 of glycolysis rearrange 3-phosphoglycerate, and how?
cards.back: Its carbon-3 phosphate is too low on the ladder to make ATP. Phosphoglycerate mutase moves it to carbon 2; enolase removes water, making PEP.
cards.quote: The remaining carbon-3 phosphate is still too low on the ladder to make ATP, so the cell raises it.
cards.section: Payoff, steps 6–10: make a phosphate worth more than ATP's, then cash it

cards.front: Enolase changes free energy only slightly, yet PEP's phosphate sits at the top of the ladder (−61.9 kJ/mol). Why?
cards.back: After the phosphate leaves, enolpyruvate is an unstable enol that quickly becomes the much more stable pyruvate, so the phosphate leaves very readily.
cards.quote: the leftover enolpyruvate is an unstable enol that quickly turns into its much more stable form, pyruvate
cards.section: Payoff, steps 6–10: make a phosphate worth more than ATP's, then cash it

cards.front: Net yield of glycolysis per glucose converted to two pyruvate?
cards.back: +2 ATP and +2 NADH (4 ATP made at steps 7 and 10, 2 spent at steps 1 and 3).
cards.quote: Net per glucose: +2 ATP, +2 NADH.
cards.section: The two ledgers

cards.front: Four phosphates pass to ADP per glucose in glycolysis. Where does the net profit of 2 ATP come from?
cards.back: Two of the four repay the ATP lent at steps 1 and 3. The other two are new, captured from inorganic phosphate at step 6 and paid for by the oxidation.
cards.quote: two are new, captured from inorganic phosphate at step 6 and paid for by the oxidation
cards.section: The two ledgers

cards.front: A glucose unit enters glycolysis as glucose-6-phosphate (from glycogen), skipping hexokinase. Net ATP per unit to two pyruvate?
cards.back: +3 ATP. Payoff is still 4 ATP (steps 7 and 10, ×2); only PFK-1 spends 1 ATP. 4 − 1 = 3.
cards.quote: Steps 7 and 10 make 4 ATP per glucose; steps 1 and 3 spent 2.
cards.section: The two ledgers

cards.front: Arsenate fully replaces phosphate at the GAPDH step. The product breaks down on its own to 3-phosphoglycerate, passing nothing to ADP. Predict net ATP and NADH per glucose.
cards.back: Net 0 ATP, 2 NADH. The oxidation still happens, but no new phosphate is captured, so step 7 makes nothing and step 10's 2 ATP only repay the 2 spent.
cards.quote: Suppose arsenate, which looks like phosphate, replaces it completely at step 6: GAPDH uses it, but the product then breaks down on its own to 3-phosphoglycerate
cards.section: The two ledgers

cards.front: Muscle breaks down glycogen (entry as glucose-6-phosphate) while arsenate fully replaces phosphate at step 6. Net ATP and NADH per glucose unit?
cards.back: +1 ATP and 2 NADH. Only PFK-1 spends 1 ATP; arsenate means step 7 makes nothing; step 10 makes 2. 2 − 1 = 1.
cards.why: Combines the arsenate result with entry below hexokinase: phosphates already on the substrate also reach ADP.
cards.quote: But no new phosphate is captured, so step 7 makes nothing, and step 10's 2 ATP only repay the 2 spent.
cards.section: The two ledgers

cards.front: Glycolysis yields about a fifteenth of the ATP of full respiration. Why do cells still rely on it?
cards.back: It is fast, needs no oxygen, and for some cells it is the only option: a red blood cell has no mitochondria.
cards.quote: But glycolysis is fast, needs no oxygen, and for some cells is the only option
cards.section: The two ledgers

cards.front: How can glycolysis stall even when glucose is plentiful?
cards.back: Step 6 uses 2 NAD⁺ per glucose from a small, fixed pool. If NADH is not turned back into NAD⁺, GAPDH stops and the payoff steps cannot run.
cards.quote: Step 6 uses 2 NAD⁺ per glucose from a small, fixed pool, so NAD⁺ must be recycled.
cards.section: Why pyruvate's fate matters: the NAD+ bottleneck

cards.front: In a sprinting muscle short of oxygen, how is NAD⁺ regenerated for glycolysis?
cards.back: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) passes NADH's electrons to pyruvate, making lactate and returning 2 NAD⁺ per glucose, so the electron ledger balances at zero.
cards.why: Yeast does the same job by making ethanol.
cards.quote: lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) makes lactate and returns 2 NAD⁺ per glucose, so the electron ledger balances at zero.
cards.section: Why pyruvate's fate matters: the NAD+ bottleneck

cards.front: A red blood cell given plenty of glucose has its lactate dehydrogenase blocked. Predict its ATP production and explain.
cards.back: It stops. With no mitochondria, LDH is the red cell's way to turn NADH back into NAD⁺; the small pool is used up at step 6, GAPDH stalls, and no payoff step runs.
cards.quote: Without it the small NAD⁺ pool is used up at step 6, GAPDH stalls, and no payoff step runs.
cards.section: Why pyruvate's fate matters: the NAD+ bottleneck

cards.front: Lactate is not a fatigue toxin. What does it do?
cards.back: Its formation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis keeps running; it travels to the liver to be rebuilt into glucose (the Cori cycle); and it acts as a signal.
cards.quote: it travels to the liver to be rebuilt into glucose (the Cori cycle), and it even acts as a signal.
cards.section: Why pyruvate's fate matters: the NAD+ bottleneck

cards.front: Which three glycolytic steps are far downhill (large negative ΔG) in the cell, and which values identify them?
cards.back: Hexokinase (1), PFK-1 (3) and pyruvate kinase (10). Their cellular ΔG identifies them; standard ΔG°′ alone does not.
cards.quote: In the cell, three steps fall far downhill.
cards.section: Control: where the cell can turn the flow

cards.front: Aldolase has ΔG°′ = +23.8 kJ/mol. Does that stop it carrying glycolytic flow forward in a red blood cell?
cards.back: No. In the cell its ΔG is near zero (about −1.3 kJ/mol), so it runs forward. Only cellular ΔG shows which steps are one-way.
cards.quote: Aldolase is the mirror case: standard value +23.8, yet in the cell it sits near zero and carries the flow forward.
cards.section: Control: where the cell can turn the flow

cards.front: Why do steps held far from equilibrium make better control points than near-equilibrium steps?
cards.back: Far from equilibrium almost nothing runs backward, so net flow equals the forward rate and changing the enzyme's activity changes flow. Near equilibrium, usually far more enzyme than the net flow needs runs both ways, so halving it barely matters.
cards.quote: Far from equilibrium, almost nothing runs backward, so the net flow is the forward rate, and changing the enzyme's activity changes it.
cards.section: Control: where the cell can turn the flow

cards.front: In a red blood cell at 37 °C, hexokinase has ΔG°′ = −16.7 kJ/mol and ΔG = −33.4 kJ/mol. Using ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q (RT ≈ 2.58 kJ/mol), estimate Q and say what it means.
cards.back: RT ln Q = −33.4 − (−16.7) = −16.7; ln Q ≈ −6.47; Q ≈ 0.0015. Products (glucose-6-phosphate, ADP) are kept scarce relative to glucose and ATP.
cards.quote: Hexokinase, for example, goes from −16.7 to −33.4 because the cell keeps its products, glucose-6-phosphate and ADP, scarce relative to glucose and ATP.
cards.section: Control: where the cell can turn the flow

cards.front: Glucose-6-phosphate builds up in a cell. Predict the effect on hexokinase, and on liver glucokinase.
cards.back: Hexokinase slows: it is inhibited by its product, so it slows when the trap is full. Glucokinase, the liver form, is not inhibited this way.
cards.quote: Hexokinase is inhibited by its product, glucose-6-phosphate, so it slows when the trap is full.
cards.section: Control: where the cell can turn the flow

cards.front: ATP is both a substrate and an inhibitor of PFK-1. How does PFK-1 respond to the cell's energy state?
cards.back: High ATP binds a second (regulatory) site and shuts PFK-1 down. When ATP falls, AMP rises and switches it back on. It asks whether the cell needs energy now.
cards.quote: When ATP is high, ATP binds a second site and shuts PFK-1 down.
cards.section: Control: where the cell can turn the flow

cards.front: Why is AMP, rather than ATP itself, a sensitive alarm signal for PFK-1?
cards.back: Adenylate kinase keeps 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP near balance and AMP is normally scarce, so a small fall in ATP raises AMP by a large fraction.
cards.quote: so a small fall in ATP raises AMP by a large fraction
cards.section: Control: where the cell can turn the flow

cards.front: What regulates liver pyruvate kinase?
cards.back: Inhibited by ATP and alanine; activated feed-forward by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate from step 3; switched off by glucagon via PKA phosphorylation. The main muscle form lacks the feed-forward control.
cards.quote: Pyruvate kinase in liver (and in red cells) is inhibited by ATP and alanine and activated ahead of time (feed-forward) by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate from step 3
cards.section: Control: where the cell can turn the flow

cards.front: Glucagon rises during fasting. Predict its effect on liver glycolysis at PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase.
cards.back: Glycolysis slows. Glucagon lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, slowing PFK-1, and PKA phosphorylation switches off pyruvate kinase. The liver makes glucose instead (gluconeogenesis).
cards.quote: insulin raises it and switches PFK-1 on; glucagon lowers it and slows PFK-1.
cards.section: Tissue wiring and carbon supply

cards.front: Why is liver PFK-1 wired to pancreatic hormones while muscle PFK-1 mainly tracks the muscle's own energy charge?
cards.back: Muscle burns glucose for itself. Liver keeps blood glucose up for everyone else, so when glucagon signals a shortage it turns glycolysis down and makes glucose.
cards.quote: Liver keeps blood glucose up for everyone else, so when glucagon signals a shortage, liver turns glycolysis down and makes glucose instead (gluconeogenesis).
cards.section: Tissue wiring and carbon supply

cards.front: Name four glycolytic intermediates that supply carbon building blocks, and what each feeds.
cards.back: Glucose-6-phosphate → pentose phosphate pathway; DHAP → glycerol-3-phosphate for lipids; 3-phosphoglycerate → serine; pyruvate → alanine.
cards.quote: glucose-6-phosphate to the pentose phosphate pathway, DHAP to glycerol-3-phosphate for lipids, 3-phosphoglycerate to serine, pyruvate to alanine.
cards.section: Tissue wiring and carbon supply

cards.front: Design an experiment to show which metabolites regulate PFK-1, and predict the results for high ATP, AMP and citrate.
cards.back: Add each to purified PFK-1 one at a time and measure initial velocity. High ATP lowers it, AMP raises it, citrate lowers it.
cards.why: Rests on ATP inhibiting at a second site, AMP activating, and citrate signaling carbon backup.
cards.quote: add ATP, AMP or citrate to purified PFK-1 one at a time and watch the velocity climb or fall
cards.section: Proving the pathway: isotope tracing and enzyme assays

cards.front: Liver cells have high citrate, which inhibits PFK-1. Predict whether carbon from dietary fructose still flows into liver glycolysis, and why.
cards.back: Yes, it bypasses that checkpoint. Fructose enters as DHAP and GAP below PFK-1 (fructokinase, aldolase B, triose kinase), below the citrate-sensitive step, though other controls remain.
cards.why: Combines PFK-1 inhibition by citrate with fructose's entry point.
cards.quote: The carbon enters below PFK-1, bypassing that checkpoint, though other controls remain.
cards.section: Fructose in the liver

cards.front: A sprinting muscle with no oxygen to spare turns one glycogen glucose unit (entering as glucose-6-phosphate) into lactate. Net ATP and net NADH?
cards.back: +3 ATP, 0 net NADH. Only PFK-1 spends ATP (4 − 1 = 3); the 2 NADH made at step 6 are reoxidized by LDH, returning 2 NAD⁺.
cards.why: Combines entry below hexokinase with the LDH electron balance.
cards.quote: When oxygen runs short, or in a cell with no mitochondria, the electrons go to pyruvate or to a molecule made from it.
cards.section: Why pyruvate's fate matters: the NAD+ bottleneck
